analysis.one_liner: Lets adults 50 to 64 buy into Medicare and allows Medicare to negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: The Medicare at 50 Act never got a markup, a vote, or a floor action in the 116th Congress; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any citizen or legal resident between 50 and 64 enroll in Medicare — the same benefits, protections, and choice of Medicare Advantage plans that people 65 and older get — paying a premium set to the average per-person cost of coverage, with subsidies for lower-income enrollees like those under the Affordable Care Act. It would also strike the part of Medicare's drug benefit law that forbids the government from negotiating prescription drug prices or setting a drug list. The bill was introduced by Senator Stabenow with 20 Democratic cosponsors and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults 50 to 64 — an age group with high rates of job loss, early retirement, and unaffordable individual-market insurance — gain a guaranteed path to Medicare coverage regardless of health status. Lower-income enrollees in that age band would get premium and cost-sharing help comparable to ACA marketplace subsidies. If the drug-pricing repeal took effect, Medicare beneficiaries generally could see drug prices set through negotiation and a drug list rather than the current no-negotiation rules.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare buy-in for anyone 50 to 64 who would qualify for Medicare at 65, with the same Part A, B, and D benefits and protections, including the option to enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan and access to the Medicare Beneficiary Ombudsman.

Enrollees who meet income criteria receive financial assistance substantially similar to the ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions they would have gotten through a marketplace plan, with the bill directing special attention to enrollees below 200 percent of the poverty line.
Appropriates $500 million per year for outreach and enrollment grants to states and nonprofits, with priority for areas at risk of having no marketplace plans at all.
Repeals the 'non-interference' provision that bars the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services from negotiating prescription drug prices or establishing a formulary under the Medicare drug benefit.
Guarantees that enrollees can buy Medigap supplemental policies without medical underwriting both at first enrollment and on any re-enrollment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would face negotiated prices and a Medicare drug list for the first time. Health insurers selling individual-market or ACA marketplace plans would lose 50-to-64-year-old customers to the buy-in, though insurers offering Medicare Advantage plans could gain the business instead. Enrollees themselves pay premiums equal to the full average per-person cost of Part A, B, and D coverage, offset only by ACA-equivalent subsidies for those who qualify, and taxpayers fund the $500 million annual outreach program.

drawbacks.text: Premiums are set at the full estimated average per-capita cost of Medicare parts A, B, and D for the buy-in population, so middle-income 50-to-64-year-olds who do not qualify for subsidies could face premiums comparable to — or higher than — the marketplace coverage the bill would displace.

The bill provides no new revenue: premiums and redirected ACA tax credits are meant to cover the program, and it directs the Secretary to ensure no negative impact on the existing Medicare trust funds, meaning it expands eligibility without adding financing to the system.

Medicaid beneficiaries 50 to 64 are barred from buying in, and people eligible for Medicaid coverage cannot use the buy-in instead, so the bill does nothing for the poorest people in this age range who would benefit most.
Buy-in enrollees are ineligible for Medicaid cost-sharing assistance, and the first coverage year could begin no earlier than one year after enactment, delaying any help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in their fifties and early sixties — the age group most likely to fall through the cracks between employer coverage, Medicaid, and Medicare — a guaranteed-issue Medicare option with subsidies would be a real safeguard, and the drug-negotiation repeal addressed a rule that has kept Medicare from bargaining on prices since the drug benefit was created in 2003. The cost side is real but modest: the buy-in is designed to be premium-funded rather than taxpayer-funded, and the main subsidy cost is redirecting ACA tax credits people would have gotten anyway. The design weakness is affordability for unsubsidized middle-income enrollees and the exclusion of Medicaid-eligible people, which limits the bill to a narrower slice of need than the buy-in idea could serve.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 — no markup, no vote, no floor action ever happened.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 13, 2019 by Senator Stabenow along with 19 Democratic colleagues.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction.

The complete action history contains only the introduction and the referral to Finance; no committee markup was scheduled, the bill was never reported out, and no vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the law barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and insurers selling 50-to-64-year-olds individual and marketplace coverage kept customers who would have had the option to switch to Medicare. Nothing changed for anyone else.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and insurers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no vote ever occurred; the bill died in the Senate Finance Committee while Republicans controlled both that committee and the Senate floor.

industries.note: Since the Medicare drug benefit was created in 2003, a statutory 'non-interference' clause has barred the government from negotiating drug prices or setting a drug list. Repealing it would have given Medicare — the largest drug buyer in the country — bargaining power that manufacturers have opposed.

Insurers selling ACA marketplace and individual plans would lose 50-to-64-year-old customers to a cheaper, guaranteed Medicare option. But the bill explicitly lets buy-in enrollees choose Medicare Advantage plans, so insurers in that channel could pick up the business instead.

The outreach program names licensed independent agents and brokers as eligible enrollment agents, funded by the $500 million annual appropriation — while barring health insurers themselves from serving that role.
